questions.prompt: Two computers exchange files directly over Ethernet, with no internet connection. Which description is most accurate?
options: They form a network only after a router supplies internet access.
They form a network only after a dedicated server is installed.
They form a network only when a third device is connected.
They form a network because interconnected devices communicate.
questions.explanation: A network requires interconnected communicating devices; internet access, a dedicated server and a third device are not prerequisites.

questions.prompt: An office lets several staff use one network printer. Which benefit does this illustrate?
options: Processor scheduling
File encryption
Resource sharing
Data compression
questions.explanation: Resource sharing lets connected users access equipment such as printers and servers. Compression and encryption concern data representation or protection, not shared access to a printer.

questions.prompt: A web server calls a separate authentication service to verify a login. In that particular exchange, what role does the web server take?
options: Proxy, because every service-to-service request uses that role.
Client, because it initiates the request to the authentication service.
Server, because its role is fixed by the service it offers browsers.
Peer, because both machines can respond to other requests.
questions.explanation: Client and server describe roles in an exchange. A machine serving browsers can act as a client when requesting another service.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a repeater?
options: Regenerate or amplify a signal
Choose routes between different networks
Store shared documents
Assign application permissions
questions.explanation: Signals can weaken as they travel. A repeater regenerates or amplifies the signal; routing between networks is a router function.

questions.prompt: An Ethernet hub receives a signal from one attached computer. Which forwarding behaviour distinguishes it from a learning switch?
options: It sends the frame to the destination port using a learned MAC-address table.
It selects the next network using the destination IP address.
It sends the frame only to ports with a matching security policy.
It repeats the signal to other ports without selecting a learned destination port.
questions.explanation: A hub is a multi-port repeater. A learning switch uses MAC-to-port information; IP routing and policy filtering are different functions.

questions.prompt: Thirty wired PCs share one LAN. You want frames for known destinations forwarded to the appropriate ports rather than repeated to every PC. Which device fits?
options: Physical-layer repeater
Wireless access point
Ethernet switch
Ethernet hub
questions.explanation: An Ethernet switch learns destination-port associations. Hubs and repeaters do not make those forwarding decisions; an access point principally provides wireless access.

questions.prompt: Two IP networks must exchange packets. Which function is required at their boundary?
options: Caching repeated application requests
Routing using network-layer destination addresses
Repeating signals to compensate for cable attenuation
Switching frames within a single local network
questions.explanation: Routing provides delivery between networks. Repeating, local switching and application caching address different needs.

questions.prompt: Which component connects Wi-Fi devices to a wired network?
options: A wireless access point
A proxy cache
A load balancer
A file server
questions.explanation: A wireless access point provides wireless devices with connectivity into the wired network. A file server supplies files but is not itself the Wi-Fi access function.

questions.prompt: Which component filters incoming and outgoing traffic using security rules?
options: A hub
A repeater
A load balancer
A firewall
questions.explanation: A firewall checks traffic against security rules. A repeater regenerates signals and a load balancer distributes work; neither is the filtering role described here.

questions.prompt: Several identical web servers should share incoming requests so one server does not carry the entire workload. Which function directly addresses this requirement?
options: Packet filtering
Signal regeneration
Load balancing
Web-content caching
questions.explanation: Load balancing distributes requests among servers. Caching may reduce repeated work but does not by itself distribute requests across the server pool.

questions.prompt: A browser sends a request to an intermediary that may return a cached response or forward the request to the origin server. Which role is illustrated?
options: Wireless access point
Proxy
Router
Ethernet switch
questions.explanation: The proxy mediates application requests and may cache content. The other devices provide connectivity or forwarding rather than the described application intermediary role.

questions.prompt: Which observation most strongly supports classifying a file-sharing exchange as peer-to-peer?
options: Participants both request and supply files without a central server organising the exchange.
Several clients request files from the same dedicated file server.
Clients reach a dedicated file server through a wireless access point.
Requests to one service address are distributed across several dedicated servers.
questions.explanation: In the decentralised peer exchange participants supply and request resources. Multiple servers or wireless connectivity do not alone make the architecture peer-to-peer.

questions.prompt: A network covering one office building is most naturally classified as which type?
options: WAN
MAN
PAN
LAN
questions.explanation: A local area network covers a small geographical area such as a building. A MAN covers a city or large campus, a WAN spans larger areas, and a PAN is centred on a person.

questions.prompt: Branches in three countries each have a local office network. What best describes the network connecting those branch networks?
options: LAN
PAN
WAN
MAN
questions.explanation: A WAN spans a large geographical area and can interconnect branch LANs. A MAN is metropolitan in scale; LAN and PAN have smaller scopes.

questions.prompt: Two systems agree on a message format but disagree on whether an acknowledgement must be sent before the next message. What is missing from their protocol agreement?
options: The same physical transmission medium end to end
Compatible sequencing and actions on receipt
A common file format for stored documents
Matching hardware from the same manufacturer
questions.explanation: Protocols specify formats, sequence and actions on sending or receipt. Agreeing only on the format leaves communication behaviour underspecified.

questions.prompt: A team replaces a network technology while keeping the service offered to the layer above stable. Which benefit of layering does this illustrate?
options: Changes can be contained behind a defined interface.
Every layer can interpret the same header in the same way.
Higher layers no longer depend on any lower-layer service.
All end-to-end functions can move into the physical layer.
questions.explanation: Layering separates responsibilities through interfaces. It reduces the impact of changes, without removing dependencies or making layer functions identical.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct OSI order from the physical medium towards the user application?
options: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical
Physical, Network, Data Link, Session, Transport, Application, Presentation
Link, Internet, Transport, Application
Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application
questions.explanation: The OSI model has seven layers. The reverse order starts at the application, while Link/Internet/Transport/Application is the four-layer TCP/IP model.

questions.prompt: A transport layer passes its data unit to the next lower layer on the sending host. What normally happens during encapsulation?
options: The lower layer replaces the transport payload with its own header.
The lower layer waits for the receiver to add all remaining headers.
The lower layer adds its own control information around the supplied data.
The lower layer removes the transport header before transmission.
questions.explanation: Each sending layer adds the control information needed for its own role. Corresponding information is processed and removed on reception rather than discarded before sending.

questions.prompt: Which OSI layer moves individual bits over the physical medium?
options: Presentation
Physical
Session
Application
questions.explanation: The physical layer deals with transmitting bits over media such as cables or fibre. Session and presentation functions operate at higher levels.

questions.prompt: Frames and MAC addresses are most closely associated with which OSI layer?
options: Data Link
Application
Session
Presentation
questions.explanation: The data-link layer handles node-to-node frame transfer and is associated with Ethernet and MAC addresses. It is distinct from network-layer packet routing.

questions.prompt: IP-based packet delivery and routing are associated with which OSI layer?
options: Presentation
Session
Physical
Network
questions.explanation: The network layer provides packet delivery from source host to destination host using addressing and routing. The equivalent layer in the four-layer TCP/IP model is Internet.

questions.prompt: Which pair of protocols belongs to the transport layer?
options: HTTP and FTP
MAC and fibre optic cable
TCP and UDP
IP and Ethernet
questions.explanation: TCP and UDP are transport protocols. The transport layer delivers data between processes; IP is associated with the Internet/network layer.

questions.prompt: Which OSI layer manages the establishment and termination of logical sessions?
options: Network
Session
Physical
Data Link
questions.explanation: The session layer manages sessions and synchronisation. Physical and data-link layers focus on transmission over the medium and between adjacent nodes.

questions.prompt: Which OSI layer is associated with data-format translation, compression and encryption?
options: Presentation
Physical
Network
Data Link
questions.explanation: The presentation layer deals with representation of data, including translation, encoding, compression and encryption in the OSI model.

questions.prompt: Which OSI layer provides user-facing network services such as file transfer and email?
options: Physical
Data Link
Network
Application
questions.explanation: The application layer supports network services used by applications, such as file transfer and email. Lower layers handle transport and delivery.

questions.prompt: In the four-layer TCP/IP model, which layer corresponds to the OSI Network layer?
options: Link
Transport
Internet
Application
questions.explanation: The TCP/IP Internet layer corresponds to the OSI Network layer. It handles IP packets and routing rather than application services or local link functions.

questions.prompt: What should a network design primarily connect technical decisions to?
options: The personal preferences of one vendor
Business and technical requirements
The newest equipment regardless of need
Only the number of ports on one switch
questions.explanation: Network design plans connectivity, hardware, security and growth around the services and constraints the organisation actually needs.

questions.prompt: A company introduces live video meetings. Which requirement deserves particular attention for interactive conversation?
options: Maximum backup-file size only
The number of printed diagrams
Low latency
The colour of the network racks
questions.explanation: Low latency reduces delay in interactive communication. Capacity and reliability also matter, but bandwidth alone does not describe delay.

questions.prompt: An organisation expects more users next year. Which design best supports scalability?
options: Use every port and all capacity immediately
Prevent new devices from joining permanently
Avoid documenting expansion options
Allow planned capacity and access-point expansion without replacing the whole network
questions.explanation: Scalability is the ability to accommodate growth without a complete redesign. It requires planning for the expected load rather than assuming capacity is unlimited.

questions.prompt: A service must remain reachable if its primary internet link fails. Which design measure most directly supports this?
options: A redundant connection with tested failover
A longer password alone
A larger monitor for administrators
A different naming convention only
questions.explanation: A redundant path and working failover reduce dependence on one link. The backup must be tested rather than assumed to work.

questions.prompt: Why separate visitor network access from internal administrative systems?
options: To make all traffic public
To control which resources visitors can reach
To guarantee visitors can access every server
To remove the need for access rules
questions.explanation: Segmentation supports security by separating groups and enforcing appropriate access between them. Separation needs suitable rules to be effective.

questions.prompt: A support team needs faster fault detection and clearer troubleshooting. Which combination best supports manageability?
options: One shared password and no logs
Adding capacity without monitoring
Monitoring, useful alerts and accurate documentation
Unrecorded configuration changes
questions.explanation: Manageability includes monitoring, configuration and troubleshooting. Alerts and documentation help staff understand and diagnose the network.

questions.prompt: Which item is most clearly a business constraint during requirement gathering?
options: The chosen IP address of a printer
The measured size of one packet
A switch port number
The available budget for the project
questions.explanation: Budget and growth plans constrain the design at the business level; technical choices should be made within those constraints.

questions.prompt: A designer checks building layouts, wiring restrictions and areas with poor wireless coverage. What is this part of?
options: Site analysis
Final stakeholder sign-off only
Replacing the requirements stage
Writing user passwords
questions.explanation: A site survey establishes physical conditions and coverage needs before detailed equipment placement decisions.

questions.prompt: Why examine peak traffic rather than only average usage?
options: Traffic patterns have no design relevance
Short busy periods may expose bottlenecks that averages hide
Averages always prove the network can handle every load
Peak measurements replace all security checks
questions.explanation: Traffic analysis should identify demanding periods and application usage, because acceptable average performance can conceal peak-time problems.

questions.prompt: A design states that employees need secure remote access but does not yet specify addresses or hardware. Which design level is this?
options: Cable installation
Device inventory only
Conceptual
Physical
questions.explanation: Conceptual design describes needed services at a high level. Logical and physical design then develop how they will be delivered.

questions.prompt: Which decision belongs most directly to logical network design?
options: The physical rack position
The length of a purchased cable
The mounting height of an access point
The IP addressing scheme and security zones
questions.explanation: Addressing, VLAN structure, routing and security zones describe logical organisation rather than the physical placement of equipment.

questions.prompt: Which item belongs most directly to physical network design?
options: The switches, access-point locations and cabling
Only the business reason for remote access
Only a statement that growth is expected
A list of desired services without implementation detail
questions.explanation: Physical design specifies the actual equipment and physical infrastructure used to realise the network.

questions.prompt: Why pilot a new design in one area before a full rollout?
options: To replace stakeholder requirements with guesses
To test assumptions and performance on a limited deployment
To avoid any testing after installation
To guarantee there can never be an outage
questions.explanation: A pilot helps identify practical issues and validate performance before expanding the deployment. It does not guarantee perfect future operation.

questions.prompt: What should network handover documentation include?
options: Only the equipment purchase price
Unlabelled screenshots without context
Logical and physical diagrams, configurations and maintenance procedures
Only a photograph of the building
questions.explanation: Useful documentation explains both the design and its operation, enabling ongoing maintenance and troubleshooting.

questions.prompt: What makes acceptance testing different from simply powering on the equipment?
options: It only checks that power LEDs are lit
It deliberately avoids realistic workloads
It happens before requirements are identified
It checks agreed requirements with stakeholders before handover
questions.explanation: Acceptance testing confirms that the deployed system meets agreed needs, such as service and capacity targets, rather than merely turning on.

questions.prompt: Which tool is suited to inspecting captured packets during troubleshooting?
options: Wireshark
A word processor
A rack diagram alone
A spreadsheet with equipment prices only
questions.explanation: Wireshark is used for packet capture and inspection. Diagrams and inventories provide other kinds of useful information.

questions.prompt: A designer starts by identifying application needs and then chooses supporting technologies. Which approach is this?
options: Hardware-only procurement
Top-down
Bottom-up
Random selection
questions.explanation: Top-down design begins with business and application requirements and derives technology choices from them.

questions.prompt: A team first selects equipment and then adapts its application plans to fit that technology. Which approach is this?
options: Acceptance testing
Traffic monitoring
Bottom-up
Top-down
questions.explanation: Bottom-up design starts with available technology and works upward towards the application and business needs.

questions.prompt: Which description best captures a hybrid design approach?
options: Ignore requirements and use only the cheapest device
Select equipment without considering applications
Assume all existing equipment must be replaced
Use business goals while also evaluating existing technology and budget constraints
questions.explanation: A hybrid approach combines requirements-led thinking with the practical opportunities and limits of available technology.

questions.prompt: In the three-layer hierarchical model, what is the primary role of the core?
options: Fast and reliable interconnection between distribution switches
Providing each end-user socket directly
Writing the organisation's acceptable-use policy
Storing every user document
questions.explanation: The core is the high-speed backbone, prioritising reliable and stable interconnection.

questions.prompt: Which layer typically aggregates access traffic and applies routing and policy controls in the three-layer model?
options: The physical cable sheath
Distribution
Access only
An application-layer web browser
questions.explanation: Distribution connects access networks to the core and commonly performs routing, filtering and policy enforcement.

questions.prompt: In a hierarchical network, where do end-user devices connect through switch ports or wireless access points?
options: Only an off-site data archive
The documentation system
The access layer
Only the core backbone
questions.explanation: The access layer provides device connectivity and related access controls, before traffic moves toward distribution and core layers.

questions.prompt: Under Zero Trust, does being inside the network automatically make a device trusted?
options: Yes; internal location grants unrestricted access
Yes; only visitors need verification
Yes; a firewall removes all internal risk
No; access still requires appropriate verification and controls
questions.explanation: Zero Trust does not grant implicit trust based solely on network location. Identity and access decisions still matter for internal devices.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of restricting connections between individual workloads?
options: To limit unnecessary access and reduce the reach of a compromise
To make every workload accessible to every user
To replace all identity checks with network location
To stop administrators from monitoring events
questions.explanation: Fine-grained segmentation controls communication between workloads. It complements identity checks and monitoring rather than replacing them.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches the lecture definition of research?
options: Copying an existing report without further investigation
Memorising facts without asking questions
Choosing a conclusion before examining evidence
Original investigation to gain knowledge and understanding
questions.explanation: Research combines original investigation with gaining knowledge and understanding. Copying or memorising alone lacks the investigative contribution described in the lecture.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best represents the structured research process in the lecture?
options: Data collection, conclusion, then invent a question to match
Choose a result, skip the design, write the conclusion
Aim, research question, design, data collection and analysis, conclusion
Conclusion, data disposal, aim, design
questions.explanation: The example begins with an aim and a research question, plans a design, collects and analyses evidence, then presents findings. The conclusion should follow the investigation.

questions.prompt: Which is a research question rather than a broad aim?
options: Learn more about teaching
Does increased online teaching correlate with changes in grades?
Identify effective teaching methods
Improve education generally
questions.explanation: The question asks about a specific relationship that can be investigated. The other options are broader intentions or aims.

questions.prompt: A researcher compares two teaching methods. Why should they control other relevant variables?
options: To reduce alternative explanations for differences between the groups
To guarantee the preferred result
To avoid collecting any data
To make the research question unnecessary
questions.explanation: Controlling other variables helps make a comparison of teaching modes more interpretable. It does not guarantee a result or replace data collection.

questions.prompt: Which project can show originality even when it studies an existing problem?
options: One that only copies the original results
One that changes the title but nothing else
One that hides the sources it reused
One that applies a different approach or technique
questions.explanation: The lecture recognises using a different approach or technique as a way to be original. Merely renaming or copying work does not introduce that difference.

questions.prompt: An experiment fails to achieve its intended outcome. Can it still contribute something original?
options: Only if the failure is concealed
No, a failed experiment cannot produce findings
Yes, investigating why it failed may produce new understanding
No, only a successful product can be original
questions.explanation: The lecture notes that by-products can be original, including understanding why an experiment or technique did not work. A failed intended outcome is not automatically the absence of a contribution.

questions.prompt: A student applies a new analytical tool to an existing problem. Which route to originality fits best?
options: Changing the project filename
Tools, techniques, procedures and methods
Copying an existing conclusion
Avoiding investigation
questions.explanation: Using new tools or procedures in a context is one of the routes to originality listed in the lecture.

questions.prompt: Unexpected results lead a researcher to investigate a new direction. Which route to originality is this?
options: Exploring the unanticipated
Repeating the expected without analysis
Ignoring the evidence
Replacing all data with assumptions
questions.explanation: Exploring unexpected findings and the new directions they suggest is described as exploring the unanticipated.

questions.prompt: Which activity illustrates originality through the use of data?
options: Copying the same interpretation word for word
Deleting data that challenges an assumption
Changing a chart colour without changing the analysis
Interpreting existing data in a new way
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies interpreting or using data in new ways as a source of originality. Cosmetic changes alone do not change the interpretation.

questions.prompt: How does the lecture distinguish information from knowledge?
options: They are defined as completely unrelated
Knowledge is simply the number of downloaded files
Information tells you what; knowledge helps explain how and why
Information explains why; knowledge is only a list of facts
questions.explanation: The lecture contrasts knowing what with a higher-level understanding of how and why. Collecting facts alone is not the same as explaining them.

questions.prompt: What does a research contribution aim to add to?
options: Only the number of files collected
The wider body of knowledge and understanding
Only the researcher's personal familiarity
Only the number of pages in a report
questions.explanation: A contribution goes beyond the researcher learning something personally: it aims to add to the wider body of knowledge and understanding.

questions.prompt: When searching for a definition of research, which approach matches the lecture activity?
options: Identify search terms, find sources and evaluate their validity
Use the first result without evaluating it
Choose whichever definition is shortest regardless of source
Avoid comparing sources
questions.explanation: The activity asks students to identify terms, use search resources, and analyse valid and current definitions. Finding a result and judging its usefulness are separate steps.

questions.prompt: Which set contains examples of original outcomes listed in the lecture?
options: Only a new physical product
Only a longer bibliography
Only an unchanged copy of a prior report
A new product, theory, model or method
questions.explanation: Originality is not restricted to physical products: the lecture also names theories, models and methods as possible outcomes.

questions.prompt: After collecting experimental data, what should the researcher do before presenting conclusions?
options: Discard all unexpected observations automatically
Rewrite the aim to guarantee success
Analyse the collected evidence
Choose the most appealing result without analysis
questions.explanation: The process includes data collection and analysis before the conclusion. Conclusions should be informed by the evidence rather than selected in advance.

questions.prompt: Which approach goes beyond merely describing a research topic?
options: Comparing explanations and testing predictions
Listing facts without examining connections
Repeating the first source found
Presenting a conclusion before gathering evidence
questions.explanation: Research develops explanations of how and why. Comparing, analysing and testing help build an argument beyond a description.

source.title: Week 2 - Good Research and Critical Thinking

questions.prompt: A finding contradicts a researcher's preferred explanation. Which response best demonstrates an open mind?
options: Stop considering alternative explanations
Examine the finding and reconsider the explanation
Exclude the finding because it is inconvenient
Keep the explanation regardless of the evidence
questions.explanation: Open-minded research allows existing ideas to be questioned. Unexpected evidence should be assessed rather than rejected simply because it challenges a preference.

source.title: Week 2 - Good Research and Critical Thinking

questions.prompt: What does generalisation concern in research?
options: Whether a report avoids specific evidence
Whether a researcher can omit the method
Whether findings may apply beyond the situation studied
Whether all participants give identical answers
questions.explanation: Generalisation considers application to other situations. The scope of a conclusion must still be justified by the research.

source.title: Week 2 - Good Research and Critical Thinking

questions.prompt: Two credible sources appear to disagree. What is the strongest next step?
options: Choose whichever agrees with your initial view
Assume both are useless because they disagree
Average their conclusions without examining their methods
Examine their evidence, context and alternative interpretations
questions.explanation: Critical analysis questions the evidence and its interpretation. Differences may arise from context, methods or the data used.

source.title: Week 2 - Good Research and Critical Thinking

questions.prompt: A report describes a rapidly changing technology using only very old evidence. Which source-quality concern is most directly raised?
options: Currency
Font choice
Paragraph length
Alphabetical ordering
questions.explanation: Currency concerns how up to date evidence is. Older work can remain useful, but its relevance to a changing context needs assessment.

source.title: Week 2 - Good Research and Critical Thinking

questions.prompt: Which addition most strengthens a position that already states a conclusion and supporting evidence?
options: State that disagreement is impossible
Consider serious objections and respond to them
Repeat the conclusion in larger type
Remove every source that disagrees
questions.explanation: Considering objections tests the reasoning and helps address weaknesses instead of simply asserting that the conclusion is correct.

source.title: Week 2 - Good Research and Critical Thinking

questions.prompt: In academic research, what does critical thinking primarily involve?
options: Accepting an argument because its author is confident
Choosing a view on impulse
Making reasoned judgements by weighing evidence and alternatives
Finding something negative to say about every source
questions.explanation: Critical thinking involves fair evaluation with grounds for judgement. It is more than criticism or personal dislike.

source.title: Week 2 - Good Research and Critical Thinking

questions.prompt: Which action best demonstrates reflective judgement?
options: Selecting the first explanation that comes to mind
Avoiding evidence that complicates the decision
Treating personal preference as sufficient proof
Considering alternatives and consequences before concluding
questions.explanation: Reflection involves careful consideration of alternatives, consequences and available evidence before drawing conclusions.

source.title: Week 2 - Good Research and Critical Thinking

questions.prompt: Which sentence makes a claim or assertion?
options: The new interface reduces task completion time.
Does the new interface reduce task completion time?
Please open the new interface.
How should we measure completion time?
questions.explanation: A claim states something as true. A question requests information, and an instruction asks someone to act.

source.title: Week 2 - Good Research and Critical Thinking

questions.prompt: Does describing a statement as a claim establish that it is true?
options: No; all claims are necessarily false
No; a claim still needs evaluation
Yes; every declarative sentence is a verified fact
Yes; using a technical term makes it true
questions.explanation: Claim describes the role of a statement, not its evidential strength. Claims may express facts, beliefs or opinions and must be assessed.

source.title: Week 2 - Good Research and Critical Thinking

questions.prompt: What distinguishes an argument from an unsupported assertion?
options: The conclusion uses more technical vocabulary
The speaker avoids giving any evidence
Reasons are offered to support a conclusion
The assertion is repeated several times
questions.explanation: An argument connects supporting reasons to a conclusion. Repetition or technical language alone does not supply that support.

source.title: Week 2 - Good Research and Critical Thinking

questions.prompt: In Toulmin's model, what is the claim?
options: The evidence collected for the argument
The assumption connecting evidence to a conclusion
An exception that limits the conclusion
The conclusion the argument seeks to establish
questions.explanation: The claim is the point or conclusion being advanced. Other parts of the argument support or qualify it.

source.title: Week 2 - Good Research and Critical Thinking

questions.prompt: A report recommends extending library opening hours and cites usage records showing heavy demand at closing time. What role do those records play in Toulmin's model?
options: Grounds
Qualifier
Rebuttal
Claim
questions.explanation: The usage records supply evidence for the recommendation, so they function as grounds.

source.title: Week 2 - Good Research and Critical Thinking

questions.prompt: What is the role of a warrant in Toulmin's model?
options: Replace evidence with the conclusion
Connect the grounds to the claim through an underlying assumption or principle
State how certain the author is
List exceptions to the conclusion
questions.explanation: A warrant supplies the bridge between the evidence and what the writer concludes from it. That link may be implicit and should be examined.

source.title: Week 2 - Good Research and Critical Thinking

questions.prompt: How does backing differ from grounds in Toulmin's model?
options: Backing states uncertainty; grounds give exceptions
Backing and grounds both mean the final paragraph
Backing supports the warrant; grounds supply evidence for the claim
Backing is always the conclusion; grounds are always objections
questions.explanation: Backing strengthens the reasoning behind the warrant. Grounds provide the evidence on which the argument's claim rests.

source.title: Week 2 - Good Research and Critical Thinking

questions.prompt: In the claim that a change will probably improve performance, what role does probably play?
options: Grounds
Backing
Rebuttal
Qualifier
questions.explanation: A qualifier expresses the strength or limits of a claim. Here it indicates uncertainty rather than an absolute guarantee.

source.title: Week 2 - Good Research and Critical Thinking

questions.prompt: Which part of Toulmin's model addresses counterarguments or circumstances that limit the claim?
options: Rebuttal
Grounds
Claim
Backing
questions.explanation: A rebuttal considers objections, exceptions or limits that the argument needs to address.

source.title: Week 2 - Good Research and Critical Thinking

questions.prompt: An argument moves from higher test scores to a claim of better understanding. Which question most directly examines its warrant?
options: Is the report title printed in bold?
Do these test scores provide a reliable indicator of understanding?
How many paragraphs does the report contain?
Which font was used to display the scores?
questions.explanation: The warrant links the scores to the conclusion about understanding. Examining whether that link is justified tests the reasoning.

source.title: Week 2 - Good Research and Critical Thinking

questions.prompt: A small study reports positive results in one setting. Which conclusion is most appropriately qualified?
options: The approach cannot fail under any circumstances
The study proves that further research is unnecessary
The approach may help in similar settings, subject to further testing
The approach will work for everyone in every setting
questions.explanation: A qualified conclusion limits its scope and strength to what the evidence can support. One setting does not establish a universal result.

source.title: Week 2 - Good Research and Critical Thinking

questions.prompt: How can Toulmin's model help when reviewing a draft argument?
options: Guarantee the conclusion is true without checking evidence
Remove the need to explain the connection between ideas
Replace every source with the writer's personal view
Identify its evidence, reasoning, limits and responses to objections
questions.explanation: The model helps examine how an argument is constructed and where it needs support. It does not itself guarantee that the evidence or conclusion is correct.

source.title: Week 2 - Good Research and Critical Thinking

questions.prompt: A review topic is too broad to cover meaningfully. Which change best narrows its scope?
options: Choose sources only by their length
Specify a particular process and geographical context
Add every related topic
Remove the research question
questions.explanation: A clear focus makes the review manageable. Boundaries such as process and location should be justified by the research question.

source.title: How to Write a Literature Review - Practical Steps

questions.prompt: Which research-note entry most helps later critical comparison?
options: Only a link with no explanation
Only whether the conclusion agrees with your opinion
Methods, findings and limitations alongside the full reference
Only a copied title
questions.explanation: Recording methods and limitations alongside findings helps you compare the strength and relevance of different studies.

source.title: How to Write a Literature Review - Practical Steps

questions.prompt: A literature review groups studies under usability, accessibility and trust. Which structure is it using?
options: Chronological
Alphabetical
Random
Thematic
questions.explanation: A thematic structure groups work by aspects of the topic so that related findings can be compared.

source.title: How to Write a Literature Review - Practical Steps

questions.prompt: A review compares what interviews and controlled experiments reveal about the same issue. Which structure best fits?
options: Methodological
Alphabetical by author
By article length
By publisher logo
questions.explanation: A methodological review examines how different research approaches influence the findings and conclusions.

source.title: How to Write a Literature Review - Practical Steps

questions.prompt: Which action demonstrates synthesis in a literature review?
options: Replace all conflicting findings with one preferred view
Combine related findings to explain agreement and disagreement across studies
List each abstract without connecting the studies
Count citations without reading the sources
questions.explanation: Synthesis connects sources into an account of the topic. It requires more than isolated summaries and should preserve relevant disagreement.

source.title: How to Write a Literature Review - Practical Steps

questions.prompt: What should a literature-review conclusion connect its findings to?
options: A new unrelated topic
The number of pages printed
The research question and the need for further research
Only the order in which articles were downloaded
questions.explanation: The conclusion draws the review together, explains its significance and relates the evidence and gaps to the proposed research.

source.title: How to Write a Literature Review - Practical Steps

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between an in-text citation and a reference-list entry?
options: The citation replaces the reference list entirely
Only direct quotations need any source details
The reference list contains only the writer's opinions
The citation identifies a source briefly; the reference supplies full bibliographic details
questions.explanation: A short citation connects a claim to a source, while the full reference gives readers the information needed to locate it.

source.title: How to Write a Literature Review - Practical Steps

questions.prompt: Before searching for articles, which step is most useful?
options: Define the information need and key concepts
Download the first hundred results
Choose a conclusion before looking for evidence
Avoid deciding what information is needed
questions.explanation: A search plan starts from the research problem, identifies key terms and considers suitable sources.

source.title: Intro to research and lit reviews

questions.prompt: Why include alternative spellings and related terms in a search plan?
options: They make a reference list unnecessary
Relevant authors may describe the same concept differently
They guarantee every result is relevant
They eliminate the need to evaluate sources
questions.explanation: Alternative terminology can retrieve relevant material that one phrasing misses. Results still need to be checked for relevance and quality.

source.title: Intro to research and lit reviews

questions.prompt: An article appears in Google Scholar. What can you safely infer from that alone?
options: Its full text must be free
Its conclusions must be correct
It still needs checks for quality, relevance and publication status
It must have been peer reviewed
questions.explanation: The lecture cautions that Scholar includes material that is not peer reviewed and may not provide free full text. Search visibility is not a quality guarantee.

source.title: Intro to research and lit reviews

questions.prompt: Which part of a journal article is usually useful for an initial relevance check?
options: The file size alone
The publisher colour scheme
The number of letters in the title
The abstract
questions.explanation: The abstract summarises the work and helps decide whether a closer reading is worthwhile.

source.title: Intro to research and lit reviews

questions.prompt: You find a highly relevant article. What is a useful way to expand the search?
options: Inspect its references for related work and recurring authors
Assume it contains everything needed
Search only sources that cite your own opinion
Discard papers with different conclusions
questions.explanation: Following relevant references can reveal connected research and key contributors. Those sources still need independent evaluation.

source.title: Intro to research and lit reviews

questions.prompt: In a search system that supports phrase searching, what is the purpose of quotation marks around "digital inclusion"?
options: Prove that each result is peer reviewed
Request the words together as a phrase
Exclude the phrase from all results
Limit every result to a particular year
questions.explanation: Phrase searching helps find the specified words together. Supported search syntax varies by platform, so check its guidance.

source.title: Intro to research and lit reviews

questions.prompt: When is a publication-date limit most defensible?
options: Only when the oldest article has a short title
When it replaces all source-quality checks
When it follows a justified boundary in the research question
Whenever it removes studies with inconvenient findings
questions.explanation: Search limits should reflect a justified scope rather than selectively hide evidence. Foundational older work may still be relevant.

source.title: Intro to research and lit reviews

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the first pass in Keshav's reading method?
options: Reproduce every experiment immediately
Check every proof line by line
Memorise all references
Gain an overview and decide whether deeper reading is worthwhile
questions.explanation: The first pass is a quick overview of the title, abstract, introduction, headings, conclusion and references to judge relevance and direction.

questions.prompt: In the five Cs of the first pass, which question concerns context?
options: How does the paper relate to other work and theoretical foundations?
How many pages does the PDF contain?
Which font is used?
What is the download speed?
questions.explanation: Context concerns the surrounding research and theoretical basis. It helps position a contribution within an existing field.

questions.prompt: What receives particular attention in the second pass?
options: Reformatting the bibliography
Figures, supporting evidence and relevant unread references
Only the paper title
Only the author's email address
questions.explanation: The second pass develops understanding of the content, including figures and evidence, without necessarily working through every detailed proof.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes the third pass in Keshav's method?
options: Ignore any missing citations
Accept the authors' assumptions without examining them
Reconstruct the reasoning or work and challenge its assumptions
Read only the conclusion again
questions.explanation: The deepest pass attempts to reconstruct the work, making hidden assumptions and potential weaknesses easier to identify.

questions.prompt: What does a concept map help you do when planning a review?
options: Guarantee that every source is reliable
Replace the need to read the literature
Determine an official assessment grade
Connect a broad topic to more specific concepts and subtopics
questions.explanation: Mapping helps organise the topic and its relationships, supporting decisions about scope and subtopics.

questions.prompt: A paragraph has accurate grammar but jumps between unrelated ideas. Which writing quality most needs attention?
options: Coherence
Correct spelling alone
Longer sentences
More abbreviations
questions.explanation: Coherence is the logical flow and connection between ideas. Correct grammar alone does not make an argument easy to follow.

questions.prompt: Which tense fits a sentence describing data collected in a completed experiment?
options: Any tense chosen randomly
Past tense
Future tense only
An imperative command
questions.explanation: Completed methods and reported past work generally use past tense. Proposed future work and established knowledge have different tense needs.

questions.prompt: A small study suggests a benefit but cannot establish a universal result. Which wording is most appropriate?
options: The result proves every alternative is useless
Obviously no further evidence is needed
The findings suggest a benefit in this sample
The method always works for everyone
questions.explanation: Cautious wording should match the scope and strength of the evidence. A limited sample does not justify universal certainty.

questions.prompt: How should an unfamiliar acronym normally be introduced in formal academic writing?
options: Assume all readers know it
Use a different expansion each time
Avoid mentioning the full term anywhere
Give the full term at first use, followed by the acronym
questions.explanation: Introducing the full term makes the writing accessible and lets the abbreviation be used consistently later.

questions.prompt: What is the best response when two sentences have no clear logical connection?
options: Clarify how their ideas relate, using an appropriate transition if needed
Insert however regardless of meaning
Add more technical vocabulary
Join them into one longer sentence without revision
questions.explanation: Signposting should express a real logical relationship. A transition word cannot repair unrelated reasoning by itself.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a primary key?
options: Identify each row uniquely
Store every relationship in one text field
Choose the display order of all rows
Allow identical identifiers for different rows
questions.explanation: A primary key identifies a row uniquely. It may contain one column or a combination of columns.

questions.prompt: An enrolment is identified by StudentID and ModuleID together. What kind of key is this?
options: A datatype
A composite key
A default value
A single-column foreign key only
questions.explanation: A composite key uses two or more columns together to identify a row. Neither column has to be unique on its own.

questions.prompt: An employee table stores ShopID to identify the shop where the employee works. Which constraint links that value to a valid shop?
options: A display format
An increment value
A foreign key
A default string
questions.explanation: The foreign key references the shop identifier, keeping the relationship tied to an existing shop.

questions.prompt: Which example illustrates data validation?
options: Changing the colour of the query editor
Sorting employee names alphabetically
Renaming a database file
Rejecting an implausible employee age
questions.explanation: Validation checks whether entered data satisfies the intended rules. The lecture uses an implausibly old employee as an example.

questions.prompt: Which datatype is most suitable for a count of whole items in stock?
options: Integer
Boolean
BLOB
Date
questions.explanation: An integer stores whole numbers. Stock counts also need suitable constraints, such as a non-negative range.

questions.prompt: Which datatype represents a true-or-false value?
options: BLOB
Boolean
Integer array
Date
questions.explanation: A Boolean represents a logical true-or-false state, rather than an image or a calendar date.

questions.prompt: Why can a numeric datatype alone be insufficient for an employee age column?
options: It prevents any positive number being entered
It automatically creates a relationship to another table
It can still accept values outside the permitted age range
It automatically verifies every business rule
questions.explanation: A datatype restricts the kind of value. A separate validation rule is needed to restrict which numeric values are acceptable.

questions.prompt: Why should database planning consider relationships as well as columns?
options: Relationships only affect the colour of a diagram
Every database must contain exactly one table
Column names alone enforce all business rules
Tables must represent how the stored entities connect
questions.explanation: Planning includes tables, columns, rules and relationships. Choosing columns alone does not describe the links between entities.

questions.prompt: A specification says every employee must have a line manager. Which design issue does this requirement directly raise?
options: How to enforce mandatory manager assignment for employee records
How to make manager names unique across employee records
How to give every manager a separate database login
How to make employee identifiers consecutive without gaps
questions.explanation: The requirement is about mandatory assignment, not name uniqueness, login accounts or the numerical sequence of identifiers.

questions.prompt: Why does the line-manager relationship refer back to the employee table?
options: The shop table stores no identifiers
A line manager is also an employee
Managers are necessarily stock items
Every employee must manage themselves
questions.explanation: This is a self-referencing relationship: one employee row can identify another employee as its manager. It does not mean an employee should be their own manager.

questions.prompt: A contact number can begin with zero and include a country-code prefix. Which choice best preserves its intended meaning?
options: Floating-point number with rounding disabled
Date with a custom display format
Text with suitable format validation
Integer with a fixed display width
questions.explanation: A phone number is an identifier, not a quantity. Text preserves meaningful characters and leading zeros; validation remains a separate requirement.

questions.prompt: A stock-price rule allows values from 0 through 1000 inclusive. Which set best tests both boundaries and the immediately adjacent invalid values?
questions.explanation: The first set tests the two valid boundary values and a value just outside each. Interior-only and invalid-only sets do not establish both boundary decisions.

questions.prompt: A title column has a default of pending. An INSERT omits that column. Which conclusion follows from the default alone?
options: The omitted column receives pending, but the title may still need review.
The row is rejected until a non-placeholder title is supplied.
The value pending becomes unique across the table.
The placeholder is replaced automatically when another row is inserted.
questions.explanation: A default supplies an omitted value. It does not validate its business meaning, impose uniqueness or schedule a later replacement.

questions.prompt: Which stock-table column connects an item to its shop?
options: Description
Shop ID
Product title
Item picture
questions.explanation: Shop ID is the foreign key to the shop table. The descriptive columns describe the item itself.

questions.prompt: A rule permits line managers with at least 90 days of service. Which expected outcomes correctly test the threshold?
options: 89 days: accept; 90 days: accept; 91 days: reject
89 days: accept; 90 days: reject; 91 days: reject
89 days: reject; 90 days: accept; 91 days: accept
89 days: reject; 90 days: reject; 91 days: accept
questions.explanation: At least 90 includes the boundary. Testing 89, 90 and 91 distinguishes an inclusive threshold from an erroneous strictly-greater-than check.

questions.prompt: Why should a designer consider what happens when a referenced employee leaves?
options: All stock prices must become zero
Every table will automatically be removed
Primary keys must always become text
Other records may still refer to that employee
questions.explanation: Dependent records can retain references to a removed employee. The design must decide how to handle those relationships and avoid invalid references.

questions.prompt: What does DROP TABLE do?
options: Removes the table, including its stored rows
Adds one new row
Changes only a selected row value
Displays all rows
questions.explanation: DROP TABLE removes a database object and its data. This is why the lecture warns that dropping objects is destructive.

questions.prompt: A sequence starts at 20 and uses INCREMENT BY 5. Which interpretation of the increment is correct?
options: Values repeat after every 5 requests.
Successive generated values differ by 5.
Exactly 5 values can be generated.
The largest generated value is 5.
questions.explanation: The increment is the step between sequence values. Limits and cycling are separate settings.

questions.prompt: A sequence starts at 10 and increments by 2. What are its first three values?
questions.explanation: START WITH sets the initial value. Adding the increment of 2 twice gives 10, 12 and 14.

questions.prompt: Which sequence setting gives its upper bound?
options: START WITH
INCREMENT BY
MINVALUE
MAXVALUE
questions.explanation: MAXVALUE sets the upper bound, while MINVALUE sets the lower bound and START WITH chooses the initial value.

questions.prompt: A sequence used for record IDs reaches its upper limit and is configured to CYCLE. What must the designer consider?
options: Wrapped values may collide with identifiers still stored.
Cycling automatically deletes rows with reused identifiers.
Cycling raises the sequence upper limit on each pass.
Cycling reserves a new unique prefix for each pass.
questions.explanation: CYCLE allows reuse of values after a limit. It does not remove existing rows or guarantee uniqueness of a key populated from that sequence.

questions.prompt: A validation rule must run when a specified database insert event occurs. Which mechanism directly associates logic with that event?
options: A stored query result
A database trigger
A column default
A sequence increment
questions.explanation: A trigger executes logic in response to a defined event and timing. Defaults supply omitted values and sequences generate values; neither is a general event handler.

questions.prompt: Which information belongs in a CREATE TABLE definition?
options: Only the final report title
The browser history of each employee
Column names, datatypes and constraints
Only the name of the database user
questions.explanation: CREATE TABLE defines the structure, including columns and their datatypes, with column or table constraints where required.

questions.prompt: A lecture provides incomplete SQL creation scripts and warns that a trigger does not work. What should you do before reusing the scripts?
options: Assume every example is a complete working solution
Run them against important data without checking
Remove all constraints to avoid reading the code
Review and test them because the lecture identifies incomplete code and a non-working trigger
questions.explanation: The final review explicitly notes missing elements and a trigger that does not work. Examples need checking against the scenario and the chosen SQL dialect.

questions.prompt: Which operation changes a table structure by adding a column?
options: ALTER TABLE
INSERT INTO
UPDATE with SET
A SELECT query
questions.explanation: ALTER TABLE changes structure, such as columns or constraints. INSERT and UPDATE change row data.

questions.prompt: Which SQL operation adds a new row to a table?
options: ALTER TABLE DROP COLUMN
INSERT INTO
DROP TABLE
CREATE SEQUENCE
questions.explanation: INSERT INTO adds data rows to an existing table. It does not create the table structure itself.

questions.prompt: In an UPDATE statement, what does SET specify?
options: The database connection password
The maximum number of tables
The columns and new values to assign
The table to remove completely
questions.explanation: SET lists the changes to apply to rows selected by the UPDATE statement.

questions.prompt: In an UPDATE statement, what is the purpose of WHERE?
options: Define a new datatype
Create a new table
Rename the database server
Choose which rows satisfy the update condition
questions.explanation: WHERE filters the rows to be changed. This allows a targeted update, such as selecting one employee by identifier.

questions.prompt: What is the usual effect of omitting WHERE from an UPDATE statement?
options: Every row in the target table is eligible for the update
The statement only updates the first row
The statement automatically adds one new row
The statement always removes the table
questions.explanation: Without a WHERE condition, UPDATE targets all rows. Check the intended scope before executing a change.

questions.prompt: What does UPDATE emp SET lastName = 'Pitt' WHERE empID = 3 target?
options: All rows except empID 3
The employee row whose empID is 3
Every employee whose surname is already Pitt
The third column of every row
questions.explanation: The WHERE clause tests the identifier value, not the physical position of the row. SET changes the surname in the matching row.

questions.prompt: What is the role of NOT NULL on an added name column?
options: Automatically supply a real name
Link the name to another table
Reject SQL NULL values in that column
Guarantee that the name is unique
questions.explanation: NOT NULL rejects SQL NULL. It does not enforce uniqueness or prove that entered text is a meaningful name.

questions.prompt: An existing employee has changed their surname. Which operation fits that task?
options: INSERT a second employee row for the same person
DROP the employee table
CREATE a new sequence
UPDATE the existing row
questions.explanation: UPDATE changes stored values in an existing row. Adding another row would create a second record rather than correct the original one.

questions.prompt: What does SQL stand for?
options: Structured Query Language
Sequential Question Logic
Standard Queue Library
System Quality Layer
questions.explanation: SQL stands for Structured Query Language. It is a language used to work with data in databases, rather than the name of one database product.

questions.prompt: Which list contains four commonly recognised NoSQL database models?
options: Key-value, document, graph and column-family
Primary key, foreign key, composite key and candidate key
Integer, Boolean, text and date
SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE
questions.explanation: Key-value, document, graph and column-family are NoSQL database models. Keys are identifiers, datatypes describe values, and SQL commands are operations. NoSQL systems vary: avoid assuming that none can represent relationships.

questions.prompt: A client gives a database designer a short initial requirements list. What is the best next step before treating it as a complete specification?
options: Clarify the requirements with the client and identify missing needs
Assume every unstated requirement is unnecessary
Choose column names and begin implementation immediately
Copy the requirements from an unrelated organisation
questions.explanation: An initial list may be incomplete. Discussion and clarification help establish what the organisation actually needs before the design is implemented.

questions.prompt: Why is communication with clients an important part of database design?
options: It helps translate organisational needs into a suitable design
It removes the need to validate the database
It guarantees the first requirements list is complete
It allows technical constraints to be ignored
questions.explanation: Designers need to understand and refine client requirements. Clear communication helps distinguish an initial request from the underlying organisational need and supports a suitable solution.

questions.prompt: A museum stores records for its collection. Which pair correctly distinguishes an entity type from one entity occurrence?
options: Catalogue ID A217; Artwork
Artwork; the catalogue-number attribute
Catalogue number; the set of all artworks
Artwork; the artwork with catalogue ID A217
questions.explanation: An entity type describes a collection of similar things; one identified artwork is an occurrence. An attribute is a property of the type.

questions.prompt: A repair service records each repair visit separately, with a date and outcome. A customer can have many visits. How should Visit be treated in a conceptual model?
options: As the relationship name replacing Customer
As one customer-name attribute of Visit
As an entity type related to Customer
As one date attribute of Customer
questions.explanation: Visits have their own occurrences and properties. Collapsing them into a single date loses multiple visits and their outcomes.

questions.prompt: Stakeholders are agreeing which things exist in a booking system and how they relate, before selecting columns and SQL types. Which model best supports that discussion?
options: Index and query-execution plan
Conceptual ER model
Physical storage layout
SQL table-creation script
questions.explanation: A conceptual model establishes business entities and relationships before more implementation-specific decisions.

questions.prompt: A publisher releases many editions. Each edition has exactly one publisher. Where does the publisher reference normally belong in a relational implementation?
options: In Edition, referencing Publisher
In Publisher, referencing one Edition
In both tables, with both references required to be unique
In Edition, replacing the edition identifier
questions.explanation: The foreign key belongs on the many side. A reference in Publisher to only one Edition cannot represent all its editions.

questions.prompt: A Member may make no bookings or several bookings. Every Booking belongs to exactly one Member. Which participation rules follow?
options: Member mandatory in booking; Booking optional in membership
Both sides mandatory
Both sides optional
Member optional in booking; Booking mandatory in membership
questions.explanation: Members can exist without bookings, while a booking cannot lack its member. Maximum cardinality and minimum participation are distinct decisions.

questions.prompt: Volunteers attend many events and events have many volunteers. Attendance stores the hours contributed by each volunteer at each event. Where should hours be stored?
options: On Event as one hours value for all volunteers
On both Volunteer and Event as duplicated totals
On Attendance linking Volunteer and Event
On Volunteer as one hours value for all events
questions.explanation: Hours depend on the particular volunteer-event pairing. An intermediate entity records each pairing and its properties.

questions.prompt: An ER model contains a many-to-many relationship. Which statement about relational implementation is most accurate?
options: Make the identifier on each side identical for every related pair.
Represent the associations using an intermediate table and related foreign keys.
Discard the relationship because relational systems cannot represent it.
Put a comma-separated list of related keys into a single field.
questions.explanation: Relational databases can represent many-to-many associations using a linking table. The slide warning concerns direct implementation, not a ban on the business relationship.

questions.prompt: Each locker is assigned to at most one member, and each member has at most one locker. No assignment is required. What relationship is specified?
options: One-to-one with optional participation on both sides
One-to-many with mandatory participation on both sides
Many-to-many with optional participation on both sides
One-to-one with mandatory participation on both sides
questions.explanation: Maximum one on both sides gives one-to-one. The permission to have no assignment makes participation optional.

questions.prompt: Which name best follows the lecture convention for a conceptual entity type representing individual loans?
options: Loans
tbl_Loan_PostgreSQL
LoanDate
Loan
questions.explanation: Loan is singular, meaningful and independent of physical implementation. LoanDate describes a property rather than the loan entity type.

questions.prompt: For the simplified conceptual ER notation used in this lecture, which deliverable fits the requested level of detail?
options: Only attribute names without relationships
Physical disk locations and access paths
Entity types and their relationships
Tables with all SQL types and indexes
questions.explanation: This lecture uses a simplified conceptual diagram of entity types and relationships, postponing attribute detail to logical modelling. Other ER notations may include attributes.

questions.prompt: A draft says each tutor supervises many projects. Which follow-up is needed to establish minimum participation?
options: Which SQL type stores a project identifier?
Can a tutor exist with no assigned projects?
What is the maximum length of a tutor surname?
Which index speeds up a project-title search?
questions.explanation: Maximum cardinality does not determine whether zero related instances are allowed. Minimum participation must be elicited from requirements.

questions.prompt: A booking design assumes every customer has already made a booking. The requirement allows customers to register before booking. What is the most direct correction?
options: Make Customer participation in the booking relationship optional.
Change Customer to an attribute of Booking.
Make the relationship many-to-many instead of one-to-many.
Remove the relationship and store bookings independently.
questions.explanation: The discrepancy concerns minimum participation, not whether customers and bookings are entities or the maximum number of bookings.

questions.prompt: Table parcel has columns parcel_id, destination and status. Which query returns only destination values for rows whose status is held?
options: SELECT status FROM parcel WHERE destination = 'held';
SELECT destination, status FROM parcel;
SELECT destination FROM parcel WHERE 'status' = 'held';
SELECT destination FROM parcel WHERE status = 'held';
questions.explanation: SELECT chooses the output column; WHERE filters rows. Quoting status as a string tests two string literals instead of the status column.

questions.prompt: A case-sensitive surname filter must match names beginning with Mar. Which condition fits?
options: surname = 'Mar%'
surname LIKE '%Mar%'
surname LIKE 'Mar%'
surname LIKE '%Mar'
questions.explanation: The trailing percent permits any suffix after Mar. A leading percent permits a prefix; percent on both sides permits a substring anywhere. Equality does not interpret the wildcard.

questions.prompt: Rows (id, city, surname) are (1, York, Marsh), (2, Bath, Marsh), (3, York, Mason), (4, York, Shaw). Which IDs satisfy city = 'York' AND surname LIKE 'Ma%'?
options: 2 and 3
1 and 3
1, 2 and 3
1 and 4
questions.explanation: AND requires both conditions. Rows 1 and 3 meet both; row 2 fails the city condition and row 4 fails the surname prefix.

questions.prompt: A query should return Bath residents whose surname starts with H. It uses city = 'Bath' OR surname LIKE 'H%'. Which error can result?
options: Residents of other cities with H surnames can be included.
Bath residents with H surnames are always excluded.
Only surnames exactly equal to H can be included.
The result necessarily contains only one row.
questions.explanation: OR accepts either condition. The requirement needs AND, so both the location and prefix must match.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL a column was created with the exact mixed-case identifier "homeCity". Which expression compares its value with the text York?
options: 'homeCity' = 'York'
"homeCity" = "York"
'homeCity' = "York"
"homeCity" = 'York'
questions.explanation: Double quotes preserve the identifier; single quotes delimit the text value. Quoting York as an identifier asks for a column of that name.

questions.prompt: A report needs parcel_id and destination for every parcel. Why prefer SELECT parcel_id, destination FROM parcel over SELECT * FROM parcel?
options: It automatically orders parcels by parcel_id.
It guarantees the query returns fewer rows.
It states the required columns and avoids returning unrelated fields.
It automatically filters out duplicate parcels.
questions.explanation: Projection controls columns, not row filtering, distinctness or ordering. Explicit columns also keep the output focused on the report requirement.

questions.prompt: Which values match code LIKE 'B%' under case-sensitive matching? Values: B, B7, AB7, b7.
options: B, B7 and b7
B and B7
B7 only
B7 and AB7
questions.explanation: Percent can match zero or more characters, so B itself matches. AB7 has the wrong start and b7 differs in case under the stated assumption.

questions.prompt: A field must preserve a variable-length external reference of at most eight characters, including possible leading zeros. Which declared type best expresses this requirement?
options: varchar(8)
integer
date
Boolean
questions.explanation: varchar(8) expresses variable-length text with a length limit. A numeric type changes the representation of leading zeros; date and Boolean describe different kinds of values.
